introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 2 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Answer ALL 10 questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated. Mathematical formulae and tables published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

questions.enonce_markdown: By using the Intermediate Value Theorem, show that the equation $x^3 - x^2 - x - 5 = 0$ has at least one real solution.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $f(x) = x^3 - x^2 - x - 5$.

* $f$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous on every closed interval, in particular on $[2, 3]$.
* $f(2) = 8 - 4 - 2 - 5 = -3 < 0$.
* $f(3) = 27 - 9 - 3 - 5 = 10 > 0$.

$f(2)$ and $f(3)$ have opposite signs, so $0$ lies strictly between $f(2)$ and $f(3)$. By the Intermediate Value Theorem there is at least one number $c$ with $2 < c < 3$ such that $f(c) = 0$. Hence the equation $x^3 - x^2 - x - 5 = 0$ has at least one real solution. $\blacksquare$

(Narrowing: $f(2.3) = -0.423 < 0$ and $f(2.4) = 0.664 > 0$, so the root lies in $(2.3, 2.4)$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Prove by induction that $12^n + 2 \times 5^{n-1}$ is divisible by $7$ for all integers $n \geq 1$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $P(n)$ be the statement: "$12^n + 2 \times 5^{n-1}$ is divisible by $7$".

**Basis.** For $n = 1$: $12^1 + 2 \times 5^0 = 12 + 2 = 14 = 7 \times 2$. So $P(1)$ is true.

**Inductive step.** Assume $P(k)$ is true for some integer $k \geq 1$: $12^k + 2 \times 5^{k-1} = 7m$ for some integer $m$. Then $2 \times 5^{k-1} = 7m - 12^k$. Now

$$12^{k+1} + 2 \times 5^{k} = 12 \cdot 12^k + 5\left(2 \times 5^{k-1}\right) = 12 \cdot 12^k + 5\left(7m - 12^k\right) = 7 \cdot 12^k + 35m = 7\left(12^k + 5m\right).$$

Since $12^k + 5m$ is an integer, $12^{k+1} + 2 \times 5^k$ is divisible by $7$: $P(k + 1)$ is true.

**Conclusion.** $P(1)$ is true, and $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$ for every $k \geq 1$. By the principle of mathematical induction $P(n)$ is true for all integers $n \geq 1$. $\blacksquare$
